newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Moody's deals Thailand a blow.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Moody's deals Thailand a blow.

text.p: Thai debt paper trading in the secondary markets weakened modestly in an already depressed market after Moody's Investors Service said it may cut the kingdom's sovereign ratings, traders in Hong Kong said Friday.
"A couple of days ago, prices were marked down, but today we are seeing some of those prices actually being hit," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
Moody's said it might cut Thailand's A2 long-term foreign currency bond and deposit ratings.
The review was prompted by concerns regarding the soundness of Thailand's financial sector as well as by constraints on macroeconomic policy-making, Moody's said.

The rating agency also said it might cut the A2 long-term foreign currency ratings of Bangkok Bank, Export-Import Bank of Thailand, Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand, Siam Commercial Bank and Thai Farmers Bank.
Traders said that while prices were quoted and some offers were taken, most players still remained sidelined.
Standard and Poor's Corp told Reuters it had no plans to downgrade Thailand, reiterating its view that the sovereign was strong enough to weather problems in the banking sector.
Traders said some of the A2 rated floating rate issues of Thai banks with tenors of three to five years were indicated at about five basis points wider than on Thursday.

Traders said the recent floating rate certificate of deposit issue of Thai Farmers Bank was indicated in the mid-30s over the London Interbank Offered Rate, a few basis points wider than on Thursday and several basis points wider than the 27 basis points all-in it offered at launch in January.
Many bankers said that Thai paper had been priced too tightly and that the recent weakening in prices was a better reflection of market sentiment.
Lower rated borrowers continue to be harder hit in the secondary marekt, even after Moody's specifically picked on the A2 rated banks in its announcement.

For example, Baa2-rated Siam City Bank, which was not put on watch, has a FRN due 2001 and puttable in 1999 that was trading around 80 basis points over LIBOR on Thursday but has widened out to 90-100 basis points.
Those notes offered a 53.3 basis points all-in return when they were launched in January 1996.

In contrast, traders said IFCT's Euro 144a bond due in 2007 was trading at Treasuries plus 85 basis points, wider than the 80 basis points it touched at its height but tighter than the 90 basis points it yielded at launch in early January 1997.
"In the Eurobonds, we're not seeing any dramatic movements, but the phone isn't really running off the hook with people trying to bid the paper," said a U.S. bank trader.
But some Eurobonds have shown significant volatility.

For instance, Thai phone operator Total Access Communication's bond due 2006 reportedly has widened some 30 basis points over the last few weeks to 195-2005 basis points over the benchmark, erasing all the gains the bond had made since its launch in October 1996.
Total Access is rated Ba1 by Moody's and BBB-minus by Standard and Poor's Corp.
Bankers said Moody's action is bad news for Thailand's planned Yankee bond, a US$500 million debut issue.
"It will definitely increase Thailand's funding costs," said one trader.
In other news, Hysan Development's HK$2 billion FRN has been launched into general syndication. The five-year notes pay an all-in return of 63 basis points ot the top tier.
Cheung Kong unit Cheung Kong Finance has increased its five-year term loan facility to HK$3.96 billion from HK$3.6 billion in the underwriting phase.
